The verse addresses all people and affirms that God's promise, namely the resurrection and recompense, is true and certain. It warns them not to be deceived by the life of this world and not to be misled about God by the Deceiver, whom most commentators identify as Satan, who encourages them to rely on God's forbearance while persisting in disobedience. Al-Tabari holds that the opening addresses the Quraysh of Mecca who denied the Prophet, and the next verse consoles the Prophet by reminding him that earlier messengers were also denied, with the final judgment left to God. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya understand the promise as the return, judgment and reward. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi explain that worldly life deceives through its pleasures, which distract from work for the Hereafter, and al-Qurtubi reports from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that deceiving about God means committing sins and then hoping for forgiveness. Al-Razi distinguishes three degrees of deception according to the strength of a person's intellect. All agree that Satan is a clear enemy who must be opposed by refusing his call, and that he drives his followers toward the Blaze. On the reading, the vowel with fatha on the ghayn is the common one and denotes Satan, while the damma form, which Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi relate to a verbal noun or a plural of a word meaning deceiver, is possible but less common. The verse closes by contrasting the disbelievers, who face a severe punishment, with the believers who do good, who receive forgiveness and a great reward.

This verse states that Satan is a clear enemy of mankind, so people must treat him as an enemy, neither obeying him nor following his whisperings. The commentators explain that taking him as an enemy means opposing him through obedience to God and resisting him in belief and deed, and that Satan calls his party only so that they end up among the people of the blazing fire. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand the "party" (hizb) as his followers and those who obey him, and Ibn Zayd, quoted by al-Tabari, says they are human beings. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Alusi argue that the lam in "li-yakunu" may express the outcome of his call rather than his primary aim, whereas al-Razi and others treat it as a hidden purpose. Al-Qurtubi cites signs of this enmity, namely the expulsion of Adam from Paradise and Satan's vow to mislead humanity. Ibn al-Qayyim notes that the command to treat him as an enemy requires constant effort to fight him. Several scholars connect the verse to the preceding warning against deception, with many taking "al-gharur" to refer to Satan himself. Ibn 'Ashur observes that this enmity calls for more vigilance than the forgiveness recommended toward human enemies, who may be reconciled. Taken together, the verse and its context call for wariness toward Satan and obedience to God.

This verse states that disbelievers will suffer a severe punishment, while those who believe and do righteous deeds will receive forgiveness and a great reward, which al-Tabari, citing Qatada, identifies as Paradise. The commentators connect it with what precedes: it follows the warning against Satan and the statement that his followers are destined for the blazing fire, and it divides the two groups.

The commentators agree that faith corresponds to forgiveness and righteous deeds to the great reward, as al-Razi notes, and that disbelief is the cause of the severe punishment, as Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi explain. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan take the phrase "those who disbelieve" as the subject of a sentence whose predicate is "for them is a severe punishment", and al-Qurtubi regards this as the best analysis. Others read it as an apposition or a complement, a view they consider less eloquent.

Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that the disbelievers are those who obeyed Satan and disobeyed the Merciful, while the believers are those who had faith in God and His messengers. Al-Zamakhshari sees the verse as a rebuke to those who rely on God's forgiveness to justify sin, while al-Razi draws a comparison with a person who accepts a brief, temporary suffering to avoid an everlasting one.

The verse comes immediately before the question about the one whose evil deeds have been made attractive to him.

This verse contrasts the person whose evil deed the Devil has made attractive, so that he sees it as good, with someone who sees things as they truly are. Allah leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills, so the Prophet should not consume himself with grief over their misguidance, for Allah knows fully what they do. Al-Tabari, al-Hasan and Qatada identify the Devil as the one who adorns their deeds, while Ibn Zayd takes hasarat to mean simple sorrow and cites a verse from az-Zumar. On who is meant, opinions differ: Ibn Abbas and others name Abu Jahl and the Meccan polytheists, Sa'id ibn Jubayr names people of desires and innovations, and Abu Qilaba names Jews, Christians and Magians. Al-Qurtubi finds the view that it refers to the Quraysh the most evident, and others mention the Kharijites. As for the implied answer, al-Kisa'i holds that it is the following clause, that your soul would perish in regret for them, while al-Zajjaj and Ibn Atiyya prefer the sense 'is he like one whom Allah has guided', and al-Zamakhshari notes both options. Al-Tabari keeps the majority reading fa-la tadhhab nafsuka, with one variant attributed to Abu Ja'far. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di stress that guidance and misguidance rest with God's will.

The commentators explain that this verse establishes God's power to raise the dead by pointing to something everyone observes in nature: God sends the winds that stir up the clouds and drive them toward a barren land with no vegetation; the rain then brings the earth back to life after its dryness and the crops grow, and so will the resurrection be. Al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir treat the comparison between the revival of the earth and the raising of the dead as the core meaning, and most of them cite the hadith of Abu Razin al-Uqayli, in which a man sees a parched land turn green and is told that God will raise the dead in the same way. On how the resurrection happens, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and those after them report that God will send down water from beneath the Throne, by which bodies will grow, while Ibn 'Ashur and others limit themselves to the aspects of the comparison without detailing the process. The readings "al-riyah" and "al-rih" differ grammatically without changing the sense. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi note that the present tense of "fa-tuthir" is used to bring the scene vividly before the listener. In the verses that follow, most exegetes link the pursuit of honour to piety: the good word rises to God and righteous deeds lift it up. They differ on what the pronoun in "yarfa'uhu" refers to: Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Mujahid say righteous deeds raise the good word, others say the word raises the deed, and Qatada says God raises it. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that the first view is the most widely held. The passage also warns against the plots of those who commit evil deeds, whose scheming will perish.

The commentators explain that this verse affirms that all honour belongs to God alone, so whoever seeks honour must seek it through obedience to Him. On the opening phrase, Mujahid takes it to mean one who seeks honour by worshipping idols, Qatada one who should make himself strong through obedience to God, and al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj one who wants to know to whom honour belongs. al-Tabari prefers the reading that the preceding verses rebuke the polytheists, so the passage urges them to abandon idolatry. As for the good word that rises to God, Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Kathir take it as remembrance, glorification and the profession of faith, while al-Hasan and Qatada hold that it is accepted only with good deeds. Most exegetes, including Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Dahhak, say the righteous deed lifts up the good word, whereas Abu Salih and Shahr ibn Hawshab reverse this, and Qatada says God Himself raises the deed. Regarding those who plot evil deeds, Abu al-'Aliya identifies them as the Quraysh who conspired against the Prophet in Dar al-Nadwa, Mujahid and Shahr ibn Hawshab as those who show off their works, Muqatil as the polytheists, while others read it generally. There is broad agreement that their scheme will come to nothing and that a severe punishment awaits them. The passage is linked in context to the rain that revives dead land, offered as evidence for resurrection.

This verse describes the stages of human creation and shows God's knowledge and power. God created the first man, Adam, from earth, then made his descendants from a drop of fluid, and then made them into pairs, male and female. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Qatada, al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, read 'from earth' as the creation of Adam and 'from a drop' as the creation of his offspring. Others, such as Ibn Juzayy, al-Nasafi and al-Razi, take it as a general address to all people, the drop itself tracing back to earth through food. The meaning of 'pairs' is debated: most understand male and female, while al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan also allow the sense of kinds or categories. All agree that pregnancy and birth happen only by God's knowledge. The phrase about a life being lengthened or shortened 'except in a Book' is discussed at length. Al-Tabari, Ibn Zayd and Mujahid take the pronoun to refer to another person, while Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Abu Malik explain it as the counting of days lived by one person. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Baydawi connect the Book with God's knowledge. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi cite the hadith that kinship ties lengthen life, and al-Alusi notes the difficulty of reconciling this with a fixed decree. All agree that this is easy for God.

This verse states that the two seas, one sweet and pleasant to drink, the other salty and bitter, are not alike, and that this difference, together with the benefits both provide, shows the power and oneness of God. The commentators differ on the purpose of the passage. Most, including al-Razi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi, read it as a parable of the believer and the disbeliever, since the two waters are not equal. Others, such as al-Razi in his broader reading, see it mainly as evidence of God's power, because the two seas differ although they share many features.

The scholars agree on the meanings of the terms: the sweet water, furat, is so fresh that it quenches thirst, and ajaj is very salty, even bitter and burning, according to Ibn Abbas, Qatada and Ibn Kathir. The fresh meat is fish, and the ornament is pearls and coral. They differ on where the ornament comes from. Ibn Kathir, al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi take it to come from the salt water, while Ibn Atiyya, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi attribute it to both waters, since springs of sweet water mix with the sea. Ibn Ashur sees the wording as a deliberate way of linking both seas in one favour.

The ships that cut through the waves are explained in different ways. Ibn Abbas and Ibn Kathir describe them as vessels that part the water with their prows, al-Hasan as heavily laden ships, and Abu Wa'il as ships crossing the waves. According to Mujahid, the purpose of this travel is trade, and giving thanks means being grateful to God for these blessings.

This verse points to God's power in the alternation of night and day: He makes the night enter the day and the day enter the night, so that one lengthens while the other shortens. He has also subjected the sun and the moon, each running its course toward a fixed term. God alone is your Lord, and sovereignty belongs to Him, whereas those you call upon besides Him do not possess even a qitmir, the thin skin around a date stone. The commentators largely agree on this meaning: al-Tabari, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Hasan take the qitmir to be the membrane or skin of the date pit. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi also report the view of Juwaybir and al-Dahhak that it is the small cone at the top of the date, a less widely held opinion. On the alternation itself, al-Tabari and Qatada see it as one period growing at the expense of the other, while al-Razi links the seasons to the movement of the sun and moon willed by God rather than to the explanations of the polytheists. Regarding the fixed term, al-Hasan places it at the Day of Resurrection, whereas al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud connect it with the duration of each orbit, one year for the sun and one month for the moon. All stress that the idols cannot hear the prayers of their worshippers, would not answer even if they could hear, and will disown them on the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi restate this point, and Ibn Juzayy sums it up: whoever owns not even the smallest thing cannot own anything greater.

The commentators explain that the verse addresses the polytheists: if you call upon the deities you worship besides God, they will not hear your call, since they are lifeless objects that neither understand nor speak. Even if they were to hear, they could not answer you, because they have no power to benefit. Al-Tabari, Qatada, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud agree that 'they will deny your association' means that on the Day of Resurrection these beings will disown your worship and deny having been partners with God, a view also reported by Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi. Al-Zamakhshari suggests the denial may also show itself through the visible inertness and helplessness of the idols. Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Juzayy hold that the pronoun could refer to angels, jinn or prophets who were worshipped, who would deny having commanded that worship. As for 'none informs you like the One who is All-Aware', most exegetes, including Qatada and al-Nasafi, take it to refer to God Himself, whose report about the deities is true. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya also allow that the address is to the Prophet or to any listener. Ibn 'Ashur observes that the preposition in 'for a specified term' can mean either reaching a limit or being destined for it, and both readings lead to the same meaning. In sum, the verse establishes the powerlessness of these supposed deities and their disavowal of their worshippers, while God alone, the All-Aware, speaks the truth.

This verse reminds people that all human beings depend on God in every matter and cannot do without Him even for a moment, whereas God is self-sufficient, needing nothing from His creatures or their worship, and worthy of praise for His countless favours. At-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain this neediness as a dependence on God's grace and bounty in this life and the next. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baydawi stress that humans are the poor in the fullest sense because of their weakness, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya note that the definite article in "the poor" intensifies this need, and that the epithet "the Praiseworthy" means His wealth is generous and beneficent, deserving thanks. The commentators agree that the following verses show divine power: were God to will it, He could remove people and bring others, which is not difficult for Him. On responsibility, at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that no one bears another's burden, not even a close relative who calls for help, though Ibn 'Atiyya adds that whoever misled others carries his own load along with the loads of those he led astray. Opinions differ on the phrase "in the unseen": some take it as fearing God in private, others as fearing an unseen God, a reading Mawardi also mentions. The commentators conclude that the warning benefits those who fear their Lord and keep up the prayer, that whoever purifies himself does so for his own sake, and that the final return is to God.

The commentators explain that the verse reminds people that they are in constant need of God, while God is independent of them. If He willed, He could cause them to pass away and bring a new creation in their place, and this is easy for Him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take this to mean a people more obedient than them, and Ibn 'Abbas describes them as people who worship God without associating anything with Him. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi add that this new creation may be other people or a world unlike the one we know. Al-Razi sees in it a proof of God's sufficiency and power, whereas al-Zamakhshari reads in it a divine displeasure toward those who took rivals to God.

Most commentators agree on the meaning of the following verse: every soul bears its own burden, and no one carries another's load, even a close relative. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada link this to sins and wrongdoings. According to Ibn 'Atiyya, the verse was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira's words to the believers. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Razi offer similar explanations, and al-Qurtubi notes a variant reading.

The commentators say that the warning benefits only those who fear their Lord although they have not seen Him and who establish the prayer. Whoever purifies himself does so for his own sake, and the final return is to God. Al-Mawardi gives two meanings of 'in the unseen': in private, or in belief in the Hereafter.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to a reminder to mankind: they are poor before God, who is self-sufficient. If He wills, He can remove them and bring another people, and this is easy for Him and not beyond His power. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi read « bi-aziz » as « difficult » or « impossible to achieve », and for God nothing of the sort is an obstacle. Ibn Abbas, as cited by al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi, specifies that God would bring after them someone who worships Him without associating anything with Him. Al-Zamakhshari sees here a divine anger caused by their rival gods and their sins, while al-Razi points to an argument from sufficiency: a king who depends on his subjects cannot easily dispense with them, whereas God can.

The exegetes agree that this passage prepares the following statement on individual responsibility: no soul bears the burden of another, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya affirm. Ibn Atiyya also mentions the occasion of revelation linked to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. Ibn Atiyya and al-Baydawi acknowledge an apparent tension with the verse in al-Ankabut about the burdens carried by the misguided, which others resolve by saying these are their own sins of misleading others. Al-Baghawi and al-Razi also discuss the grammar of the verbs and adjectives, while Ibn Ashur holds that the verse recalls God's will to renew the believing people rather than to destroy them.

This verse states that every soul bears only its own burden on the Day of Judgment, and that no one is punished for another's sin. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that a person weighed down by sins who calls upon someone to carry some of that burden will find no one to help, even if the one called is a close relative such as a father, mother or brother. Ibn Kathir cites the verse about a man fleeing from his brother, mother and father on that day. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy see in this a proof of divine justice and note that the text excludes any bearing of another's load. The verse that says misguiders will carry their own burdens along with others' burdens is, according to al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan, not a contradiction, since it refers to those who lead others astray, whose loads come from their own deeds. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi note that the warning benefits especially those who fear their Lord in secret and keep the prayer, since they are the ones who profit from admonition. Al-Mawardi and Ibn Juzayy explain the phrase "in the unseen" as fearing God when one is out of people's sight, while Ibn 'Ashur reads it as sincere fear without display. On purification, al-Tabari and Qatada take it as repentance and faith, while Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi understand it as abandoning sins and doing good deeds. All the commentators agree that whoever purifies himself does so for his own benefit, and that the final return is to God.

This passage states that the blind and the seeing are not equal, nor are darkness and light, shade and scorching heat, or the living and the dead. Most commentators read these pairs as images for the believer and the disbeliever. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya explain that the blind man is the disbeliever and the seeing man the believer, with darkness standing for unbelief and light for faith. Al-Tabari also reports that shade is understood by some as Paradise and scorching heat as Hell. Al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi record another reading, in which the blind man is the ignorant and the seeing man the knowledgeable. On the word harur, Ibn Atiyya rejects Ru'ba ibn al-Ajjaj's view that it is a night wind distinct from the samum, while al-Qurtubi follows al-Farra' and al-Nahhas in holding that harur occurs both by night and by day. For the living and the dead, Qatada sees believers and disbelievers, while Ibn Qutayba sees the wise and the foolish. The verse 'you cannot make those in the graves hear' is read by most as meaning that disbelievers, whose hearts are dead, do not respond to guidance, and that the Prophet's duty is only to warn, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi state. Ibn Atiyya also raises the question of whether the dead hear, citing the well-known incident of the wells of Badr, without settling it.

This part of the verse states that darkness is not equal to light, just as the blind man is not equal to the one who sees. The commentators generally read darkness as disbelief and error, and light as faith and guidance. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and others take the verse as an image of the believer and the disbeliever. Al-Tabari holds that the darkness of disbelief and the light of faith are not alike, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn Juzayy add that truth and falsehood, with their respective rewards and punishments, are what is meant.

The scholars differ over the meaning of harur, the scorching heat. Al-Farra' says it occurs both by night and by day, whereas Ru'ba limits it to night and the samum to day. Abu 'Ubayda links it to the heat of the sun. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan record these opinions without settling between them, though Ibn 'Atiyya notes that the samum is specific to daytime.

There is also agreement that the repeated particle 'la' (not) strengthens the negation. Al-Akhfash, as cited by al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi, considers it superfluous, while others treat it as a true negation. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di draw the lesson that opposites are not equal. Al-Razi and al-Biqa'i explain the repetition of the negation, and the singular form used for light, by the multiplicity of the paths of error against the unity of the truth.

In this verse God states that the blind and the seeing are not equal, nor are darkness and light, nor shade and the scorching wind. Most commentators apply these images to the believer and the disbeliever: the disbeliever is like the blind man in the darkness of unbelief, and the believer like the seeing man in the light of faith. Qatada and Ibn Zayd read all of these as parables for the believer and the unbeliever, the one with a living heart and the other with a dead one. Others, such as al-Suddi and Ibn 'Abbas, take the shade to mean Paradise and the scorching wind to mean Hell, that is, reward and punishment. On the word harur, the linguists differ: al-Farra' and al-Nahhas say it can occur by night as well as by day, while the simum occurs only by day; Abu 'Ubayda ties it to the sun of the day; Ru'ba says it is nocturnal and the simum diurnal. Al-Tabari concludes that it occurs both night and day but that here it means the heat that accompanies the sun, since shade only exists with the sun. Regarding the living and the dead, some take them as believers and unbelievers, others as the wise and the ignorant, and the grammarians debate the role of the repeated particle la. In the phrase that God makes whom He wills hear, most understand it as guiding whom He wills, while those in the graves refer to unbelievers whose disbelief has deadened their hearts, so the Prophet cannot make them hear; his task is only to warn, and guidance belongs to God, as al-Tabari and al-Zamakhshari explain.

This verse states that the blind and the seeing are not equal, nor are darkness and light, shade and the scorching heat, or the living and the dead. Most commentators read it as a comparison between the believer and the disbeliever. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that the believer is seeing and alive, walking in light, while the disbeliever is blind and dead, in darkness. Al-Tabari adds that darkness and light stand for disbelief and faith. For the shade and the harur, many take them as Paradise and Hell, while al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayda understand the harur as the heat of the sun or a hot wind; they differ on whether it occurs by night or by day, and al-Nahhas, followed by al-Qurtubi, holds that it can happen both. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi and al-Kalbi offer closely related meanings.

The phrase that God makes whom He wills hear is understood by most as hearing that leads to guidance and acceptance, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi state. Al-Zamakhshari holds that God guides those He knows will benefit from guidance. Ibn al-Qayyim argues that the verse denies that the disbeliever benefits from being made to hear, not hearing as such. Al-Razi gives two readings: distinguishing the hearing of unbelievers from that of the dead, or consoling the Prophet. Some report that 'A'isha held that the dead do not hear, while 'Umar and his son, relying on the account of Badr, held that they do, as al-Qurtubi and al-Baghawi record.

All agree that the Prophet is only a warner who delivers the message, and that God sent a warner to every nation.

This passage establishes that the Prophet ﷺ's mission is only to warn and convey the message, while guidance rests with God alone. The commentators first agree that the blind and the seeing are not equal, nor are darkness and light, shade and scorching heat, or the living and the dead. For most, these images stand for the believer and the disbeliever, as Qatada and Ibn Kathir explain. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi instead read the shade and the scorching heat as Paradise and Hellfire. Al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayda differ on the meaning of harur, some taking it as the night wind, others as the heat of the day sun. All agree that God making whom He wills to hear means He guides whom He wills so that he hears the proof and accepts it, and that the disbelievers are like the dead in their graves because they gain nothing from admonition, as al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir state. On 'you are only a warner', al-Tabari and al-Nasafi hold that the Prophet's duty is to deliver and warn, and that whoever God wills to guide will listen and be guided. A grammatical question concerns the repeated particle 'la' in the list: some Basran grammarians treat it as an emphatic addition, others as a separate negation. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya observe that the verse consoles the Prophet and obliges the people to accept his message, since he is no innovation among the messengers. Ibn 'Ashur reads it as a justification of the Prophet and a consolation for the loss of his counsel among the unbelievers. The general sense is shared: warning is the messenger's role, and guidance belongs to God.

This verse states that God sent His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ with the truth, as a bringer of good news to those who believe and a warner to those who reject. It adds that no community has ever existed without a warner who came before, so his mission is not something unprecedented. The commentators explain that the truth means faith in God and the laws of religion, that good news refers to Paradise for those who believe and obey, and that warning refers to punishment for those who disobey. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi largely agree that the warner is a prophet or messenger who admonished his people, and that every nation received a call. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy note that only the warning is mentioned because it is always accompanied by good news, and that a community may mean a large group linked by a common descent. The meaning of the word umma is debated: al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi take it to mean the people of one era, while Ibn 'Ashur understands a large lineage-based group. Al-Qurtubi reports that Ibn Juraij excludes the Arabs from this generality, and Ibn al-Jawzi mentions that some regard the verse as abrogated by the verse of the sword. For al-Razi and others, the passage mainly consoles the Prophet over his people's rejection, reminding him that earlier messengers faced the same fate. Ibn 'Uthaymin stresses the mercy in this mission and the value of truth in both information and judgment. No commentator draws a specific legal ruling from this verse.

In this verse God consoles His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: if his people call him a liar, previous nations also called their messengers liars, though those messengers had brought them clear proofs, scriptures and the illuminating Book. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that the zubur are writings and that the enlightening Book is the clear text. Al-Razi, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi see in the three terms a gradation of evidence according to the rank of the messengers: miracles for all, books of admonition for some, and a Book carrying laws for the highest. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Nasafi hold that the terms may refer to one reality, the repetition serving to emphasise its attributes, and al-Qurtubi notes that the repeated words may differ only in wording. Ibn 'Ashur observes that the sentence distributes the different signs among the different prophets. All agree on the consoling sense of the verse and on the warning to the disbelievers: those who rejected their messengers were destroyed. Ibn 'Uthaymin adds that the miracles were suited to each prophet's era, such as Moses' staff against sorcery, Jesus' medicine, or the eloquence of the Qur'an.

The commentators explain that this verse follows the consolation of the Prophet ﷺ over his people's denial. God reminds him that earlier nations also denied their messengers, who came with clear signs, scriptures and the illuminating Book, and that God then seized those who disbelieved. The phrase « how was My rejection » means: how was My disapproval and punishment. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Jalalayn agree that it is a warning to the Quraysh, who would meet the same fate if they persisted. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan hold that the signs, the scriptures and the illuminating Book may be one reality repeated for emphasis, while al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur see distinct categories: miracles, written admonitions, and laws revealed in books, which Ibn 'Ashur links to different prophets. Ibn 'Ashur also explains that « seizing » means destruction and that « nakir » denotes severe punishment. Al-Razi says the question is rhetorical, reminding listeners of a punishment they already know. The commentators agree on the core meaning; they differ mainly over how the terms are classified.

God tells His Prophet that He sends down water from the sky and brings forth fruits of varied colours from it, a sign of His power and wisdom, since all are watered by one water yet yield different fruits. Most commentators take the colours to be red, yellow, green and black, while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Alusi note that they may also mean kinds and species, and Ibn 'Ashur stresses the variety of types within a single kind. The juddun are streaks or bands in the mountains. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir describe them as white and red streaks, and al-Tabari cites a verse of Imru al-Qays about the stripe on a donkey's back. As for the ghara-ib, al-Mawardi, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn al-Jawzi report three readings: black mountains according to al-Suddi and Ikrima, black bands according to Ibn 'Abbas, and black valleys according to Qatada. All agree that ghirbib means very intense black, but they differ on word order: al-Farra' speaks of inversion, while Abu Hayyan and others take sud as an appositive. The same variety appears among people, animals and livestock. The verse then links fear of God to scholars: Ibn 'Abbas and al-Tabari take them to be those who know God's power, while al-Rabi' ibn Anas says whoever does not fear God is not a scholar. Al-Zamakhshari adds that knowledge grows with fear. The verse ends by stating that God is mighty and forgiving.

This verse presents the variety of colours among humans, animals and beasts, as among fruits and mountains, as a sign of God's power and wisdom, though they share a common origin, and the commentators take it as a lesson for those who reflect. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the colours include black, white, red and yellow, and that the 'dawabb' are whatever crawls on the earth apart from humans and livestock, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya read the sense as 'and among them are some whose colours differ'. The commentators agree that the fear of God meant here (khashya) is an awe grounded in knowledge of God and His greatness, and that knowledge is its path. Ibn Abbas, cited by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, says the scholars are those who know that God is capable of all things, and Ibn Mas'ud says that abundance of this fear is itself knowledge. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi see the placing of God's name first as restrictive: it is only the scholars among His servants who fear Him. They also record a reading attributed to Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz and Abu Hanifa, with God in the nominative and 'the scholars' in the accusative, which they understand to mean reverence. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note that ending with 'the Mighty, the Forgiving' joins fear and hope. Ibn Ashur holds that 'innama' here restricts the point against the ignorant among the polytheists. Ibn Uthaymin considers that this fear is the highest kind of fear and that the verse shows the excellence of knowledge, since it is the cause of such fear.

This verse describes those who constantly recite the Book of God, establish the prayer, and spend from what He has provided, both secretly and openly. They hope for a trade that will never fail, meaning a reward from God that will never run out. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand recitation as reading the Quran together with acting on it, and establishing the prayer as performing it at its times with all its conditions. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan add that recitation also means following what the Quran teaches. The commentators agree that spending includes both obligatory charity and voluntary giving. Al-Baydawi reports the view that secret giving applies to voluntary charity and open giving to the obligatory kind, while al-Alusi and Ibn 'Ashur leave the choice to the circumstances. The word commerce is taken by most to mean seeking reward through obedience, and the phrase that will never perish means it will neither fail nor be lost. On the extra reward, Ibn 'Abbas relates it to what no eye has seen nor ear heard, while al-Mawardi lists several interpretations, including multiplied good deeds and intercession. The verse ends with God being Forgiving and Appreciative, which Qatada and Ibn 'Abbas explain as His forgiveness of great sins and His appreciation of small good deeds.

This verse describes those who recite the Book of God, establish the prayer, and spend from what God has given them, both secretly and openly. They hope for a trade that will never fail, which is God's reward. The commentators explain that God will pay them their wages in full and add to them out of His bounty. They also note that God is Forgiving of their faults and Appreciative of their deeds, meaning He rewards a little with much. Most commentators understand the added bounty as multiplication of good deeds, as Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi do. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Mawardi also cite other meanings: widening of the grave, intercession for those one has helped, and the sight of God's face, while Ibn Abbas is reported to have said it means blessings no eye has seen. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi likewise mention intercession. Mutarrif ibn Abd Allah called this the verse of the reciters. On the meaning of recitation, some scholars such as al-Zamakhshari take it as reading, others as following and acting on what the Book contains. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi explain God's appreciation as accepting small acts and rewarding them generously. The verse thus promises a generous reward to those who combine worship with charity.

In this verse God affirms that the Qur'an He revealed to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is the truth, free of any falsehood, and that it confirms the scriptures that came before it. The commentators explain that the Book is the Qur'an, and that the word "from" is explanatory according to most of them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya specify that the earlier books are the Torah, the Gospel and other scriptures, and that the Qur'an bore witness to their truth, especially by affirming prophethood and the divine origin of those books. The closing phrase, "Indeed, Allah is ever Acquainted and Seeing of His servants," is understood by most as an affirmation of God's knowledge of the inner and outer states of people. Al-Razi, Al-Nasafi and Al-Baydawi draw an argument from it: had there been anything in the Prophet inconsistent with his mission, God would not have revealed to him such a miraculous Book, which serves as a measure for all others. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan note that mentioning the All-Aware before the All-Seeing points to matters of the heart as the essential concern. Ibn Sa'di adds that earlier laws suited their own times and that God closed revelation with Islam. The commentators agree that the verse reassures believers and warns those who reject, since God knows each person and will repay them according to what they deserve.

This verse says that God gave the Book as an inheritance to those He chose from among His servants, and divided them into three groups: one who wrongs himself, one who is moderate, and one who outstrips others in good deeds by God's leave. The commentators disagree about who these chosen ones are and what the three groups mean. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Ka'b al-Ahbar, 'A'isha and many others, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy, understood them to be the community of Muhammad ﷺ: the one who wrongs himself is the person who commits sins, the moderate one fulfils the obligations and avoids major sins, and the foremost one multiplies his acts of devotion. Reports attributed to the Prophet ﷺ, 'Umar and 'Uthman state that all three groups will enter Paradise, a view that al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir seem to favour. By contrast, al-Hasan al-Basri, Qatada and 'Ikrima held that the one who wrongs himself is the hypocrite or the disbeliever, and that the moderate and the foremost are believers; al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya also adopted this reading in some of their remarks, relying on the parallel in surat al-Waqi'a. Mujahid likened the three groups to the people of the left hand, the right hand and the foremost of the sura al-Waqi'a, while Ibn 'Abbas took the foremost as the sincere believer and the moderate as the showy one. The Book is generally taken to mean the Qur'an, although al-Mawardi and al-Tabari also considered the earlier scriptures as a whole. Some explained that the one who wrongs himself is named first so that he keeps hope, and the foremost is named last so that he does not feel vain about his works. The phrase 'by God's leave' is read as a reminder that success depends on His support, and the closing words 'that is the great bounty' refer to God's choosing or to the granting of the Book.

This verse describes the Gardens of Eden that those who were given the Book will enter, where they will be adorned with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their clothing will be silk. The commentators see these adornments as part of the bliss of Paradise. Al-Razi treats them as additional jewelry given to the chosen ones, while al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi note that the pearls may be set in gold. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir point out that silk is forbidden to men in this world but permitted in the hereafter. When the chosen say, 'Praise be to God who has removed grief from us,' the scholars differ on which grief is meant. Ibn Abbas and Ikrima say it is the fear of the Fire and of having deeds rejected, Ata says the fear of death, Qatada the troubles of this world, Sa'id ibn Jubayr the worries about bread, and al-Zajjaj any anxiety about livelihood or the afterlife. Al-Tabari concludes that all forms of grief are removed. On the one who wrongs himself, Ibn Abbas, Ikrima, al-Hasan and Qatada take him to be the disbeliever, while Umar, Uthman, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu al-Darda', A'isha and Abu Sa'id take him to be the believer who committed lesser sins, all of them entering Paradise. Ibn Kathir follows this latter view and cites several reports supporting it, some of which he considers weak.

This verse reports that the people of Paradise, once they have entered it, adorned with bracelets of gold and pearls and clothed in silk, praise God for removing sorrow from them and say that their Lord is forgiving and grateful. The commentators agree that the word 'sorrow' covers every kind of grief, but they differ on which sorrow is meant. Ibn 'Abbas took it to be the fear of the Fire, and Qatada the fear of death, a view Atiyya also reported. Samura and Shamir saw it as anxiety over livelihood and bread, al-Qasim as fear of losing blessings and of an uncertain outcome, and Muqatil as the distress of departing to the afterlife. Abu al-Darda' linked it to the terrors of the Day of Resurrection and the anguish of the one who wronged himself. Al-Tabari preferred the general sense, since God specified no particular kind of sorrow, and Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Kathir agreed. Al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi list further views, such as hunger, fear of rulers, or envy. On the phrase 'forgiving and grateful', some explain that God forgives many sins and rewards even small good deeds. The commentators also note that entering Paradise is a favour of God and not earned by deeds alone, and that it is an abode of lasting residence where no weariness or fatigue touches its people.

This verse records the words of the people of Paradise once they are settled there: praise belongs to God, who has made them dwell in the abode of permanence by His bounty, so that no toil or weariness touches them. Al-Tabari explains that the abode of permanence is the place one never leaves, and that the vowelled form al-muqama means the dwelling itself. Qatada reads it as a place where people do not move. The word nasab denotes bodily toil or pain, and lughub the exhaustion that follows it, as Ibn Atiyya, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baydawi explain. Ibn Abbas and Qatada take nasab as weariness or pain, while al-Razi holds that naming exhaustion after toil is a graded negation, since a person can tire without effort.

The commentators agree that this dwelling is granted by God's favour and not as a strict wage for deeds. Al-Zamakhshari distinguishes this bounty from mere reward, and Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya cite the hadith that no one enters Paradise by his deeds alone. The verse follows directly on the words that God has removed their grief, and the commentators list many possible meanings of that grief: fear of Hell, dread of death, anxiety over provision, and the terrors of the Day of Judgement. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir note that the word covers every kind of sorrow.

For these readers, the verse describes a permanent rest in which weariness has no place, and gratitude to God is its natural expression.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the state of the disbelievers in Hell: no decree of death will be issued against them so that they might rest, and their punishment will not be lightened, for this is how every ungrateful disbeliever is repaid. Several scholars note that death would have been a relief to them, which is why they wish for it without receiving it, as the verse of the guardian Malik shows. Ibn al-Jawzi cites al-Hasan al-Basri's view that they neither die nor live, while most exegetes understand that no second death will be decreed to bring them rest. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain the subjunctive of "fayamutu" by the implied particle "an", while Abu Hayyan reads it as the absence of the cause leading to the absence of the effect. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari stress that the punishment is continuous; al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya argue that the phrase about the fire being rekindled does not contradict this, since it refers to the kind of punishment rather than its exact instance. Their cries, according to al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, are a plea to be returned to the world to do righteous deeds, and they are rebuked that God gave them a lifespan long enough for reflection. Opinions differ on the length of that lifespan: Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ali said sixty years, al-Hasan and Masruq forty, and Qatada and 'Ata eighteen; al-Tabari preferred forty. As for the warner, most scholars identify him as the Prophet, while 'Ikrima and Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna take it to be grey hair, and others mention fever or the death of relatives. The commentators agree that the verse is a warning to the thoughtful to take heed before it is too late.

This verse describes the fate of those who disbelieved in the Fire. They cry out there, asking God to bring them out so that they may do righteous deeds other than what they used to do. They are then rebuked: were you not given a life long enough for whoever wished to be mindful to be mindful, and did not the warner come to you? So taste the punishment, for the wrongdoers have no helper. The commentators agree that the disbelievers do not die in the Fire and that their punishment is not lightened, and that their cries are an admission that their deeds were evil. They differ on the length of life that allows reflection. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ali and Abu Hurayra, as Ibn Kathir reports through the hadith, set it at sixty years, while Ibn 'Abbas in another report, Masruq and al-Hasan set it at forty, al-Hasan also mentioning puberty, and Qatada and 'Ata at eighteen. As for the warner, most scholars identify him as the Prophet, peace be upon him, while 'Ikrima, Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna and Waki' say it means white hair, and others mention fever, the death of relatives or full intellect. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir favour the messenger, since proof is established through the prophets. Some explain the endlessness of the punishment by God's knowledge of the disbelievers' persistence in disbelief. Ibn 'Ashur notes that wrongdoing includes polytheism and that the absence of any helper applies to every wrongdoer.

In this verse God affirms that He knows the unseen of the heavens and the earth, meaning everything hidden from the senses in both realms, and that He knows what the breasts conceal, the intentions and inner beliefs that no one else perceives. The commentators read it as a justification for what precedes it: if God knows what is in the hearts, which is the most hidden, He knows all the rest all the more. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi agree that "what is in the breasts" refers to the thoughts and beliefs people conceal. Al-Zamakhshari explains that "dhat" is here the feminine of "dhu", meaning "accompanying", since the inner states accompany the breasts as the fetus accompanies the belly. Al-Tabari reads in it a warning against doubt, whether about God's oneness or about Muhammad's prophethood. Al-Razi connects this knowledge to the duration of the unbelievers' punishment: God knows their disbelief is so rooted that they would never have believed even had they lived forever, so their torment lasts without end. Ibn 'Ashur sees a reassurance for the Prophet: God repays each person according to what he has hidden. The commentators agree on the central meaning of the verse and differ mainly on how to connect it with what comes before.

This verse states that God made you successors on the earth, each generation replacing the one before. Whoever disbelieves bears the burden of his own disbelief alone, and disbelief only increases the disbelievers in hatred from their Lord and in loss. The commentators agree that this succession means each people follows those who came before, and that it should prompt reflection on the fate of earlier nations. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take the address to be to humankind in general, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi read the succession as God granting people the disposal of the earth and its benefits so that they might give thanks. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi add that a later generation, having seen what happened to earlier ones, should take a lesson from it. Al-Razi links the verse to the preceding argument: God granted time, reason and a messenger, so disbelief after all this is most deserving of blame. On the word maqt, most explain it as intense hatred, al-Jalalayn and Ibn Juzayy rendering it as anger or contempt, and al-Tabari as distance from God's mercy. All agree the loss meant is the loss of the hereafter, some adding that it extends to souls and kin on the Day of Resurrection.

God instructs His Prophet ﷺ to challenge the polytheists about the partners they invoke besides God: what have they created from the earth, do they share in the creation of the heavens, or has God given them a Book providing clear proof? The commentators understand the expected answer to be no on all three counts: no creation, no partnership, and no scripture. Al-Tabari, Qatada, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi agree that the aim is to refute polytheism and establish the case against the disbelievers. Al-Tabari takes the pronoun in 'given them' to refer to the polytheists, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi allow that it may refer to the partners, al-Razi giving both readings. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi record the variant readings of 'bayyina' and 'bayyinat', and al-Qurtubi prefers the plural as matching the 'Uthmanic codex. As for 'the wrongdoers promise one another only delusion', most take it to mean leaders assuring their followers that the idols will intercede with God, whereas al-Mawardi and Ibn 'Atiyya also mention a promise of victory over the Muslims. Al-Alusi and Ibn 'Uthaymin extend the verse to any falsehood made attractive by its adherents. The passage then turns to God's power in holding the heavens and earth from collapsing; Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi read the divine forbearance and forgiveness as God's patience in delaying punishment, while Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi note that the feared collapse will occur on the Day of Resurrection or is presented as a hypothetical.

The commentators explain that the verse affirms God's power to hold the heavens and the earth so that they do not collapse, and that if they were to vanish, no one but Him could hold them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari read the verb as meaning to prevent, while Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baydawi note that the phrase 'if they were to cease' may be hypothetical or refer to the Day of Resurrection, as Ibn Juzayy also reports. The closing words, 'Indeed He is Forbearing and Forgiving', are explained by commentators such as al-Sam'ani and al-Zamakhshari as God's restraint in delaying punishment, even though polytheism was grave enough to shatter the heavens, in line with the comparison in Surah Maryam.

All agree that the verse comes after a refutation of idolatry: the false deities cannot create anything on earth or in the heavens, and the promises of intercession that the wrongdoers make to one another are vain. Al-Razi develops this argument by showing that the world can be sustained only by God.

The main point of disagreement concerns the rotation of the heavens. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari cite Ibn Mas'ud's rejection of Ka'b al-Ahbar's claim that the sky turns on the shoulder of an angel, arguing that the verse contradicts it. Al-Alusi reports that most of the early scholars held that the heavens do not turn and are distinct from the celestial orbits, while many later scholars identify them with the orbits. Ibn 'Ashur links the sustaining of the heavenly system to the laws of gravitation without deciding the question of rotation.

Ibn Kathir also cites a narration about Moses and God's sleep, which he judges to be an unreliable Israelite report, whereas Ibn al-Qayyim reads it as an image of divine patience.

The verse reports that the Quraysh swore their most binding oaths, before the Prophet ﷺ was sent, that if a warner came to them they would be better guided than any of the nations, meaning the Jews and Christians who had rejected their messengers. When Muhammad ﷺ came, his coming only increased their aversion to the truth. The commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur, agree that the warner is the Prophet ﷺ and that 'nufur' means turning away from guidance. Al-Tabari and al-Zamakhshari take 'arrogance on earth' as an object of purpose or an apposition to 'aversion', while al-Razi also reads it as a state. As for 'evil scheming', Qatada and Ibn 'Abbas understand it as associationism, while al-Mawardi also gives the scheming against the Prophet and his religion. On the reading of Hamza and al-A'mash that drops the final vowel of 'as-sayyi'', al-Zajjaj considers it a solecism, whereas Abu 'Ali al-Farisi justifies it as pause applied in connection. The surah concludes that evil scheming falls only upon its people, and that God's way admits no change and no transfer of punishment to those who did not deserve it. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi cite the hadith forbidding deceit in this connection, and Ibn 'Ashur sees the verse as a closing admonition.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the end of the disbelievers' arrogance and scheming. Before the Prophet's mission, the Quraysh had sworn that if a warner came to them they would be better guided than the earlier nations; yet when the warner came, it only increased their aversion. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi agree that arrogance on earth means rejecting the truth, and that the 'evil scheming' is shirk and turning people away from faith, which may include harming the Prophet and the believers. As for the phrase 'the evil scheme encompasses only its authors', most take it to mean that the harm of the scheme returns upon those who devise it; some link this to the battle of Badr, while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi read it in general terms. The reading of 'as-sayyi' with a silent hamza by Hamza and al-A'mash divides the grammarians: al-Zajjaj calls it a grammatical error, whereas Abu 'Ali al-Farisi and al-Qushayri explain it as a pause or the application of stopping pronunciation to connection. Al-Razi reads the question 'do they await anything' as waiting, and the 'custom of the ancients' as the punishment of the deniers; God's custom can neither be replaced nor transferred from its rightful recipients. Ibn 'Abbas, as reported by al-Baghawi, holds that the consequence of shirk falls only on those who commit it, and Ibn Kathir cites a report involving Ka'b and Ibn 'Abbas about whoever digs a pit for his brother. The exegetes broadly see in the verse a warning to the arrogant and deceitful and a consolation for the Prophet, while differing on the details of the scheme and of the warner.

This verse calls the idolaters to travel through the land and reflect on the fate of earlier peoples who denied their messengers, peoples who were stronger than them yet were not spared when punishment came. The commentators explain that travelling may mean reflection on history or physical visits to the ruins of destroyed nations. They also state that no one can escape God on earth or in the heavens, because His knowledge and power are complete.

Most commentators agree that the addressees are the Quraysh and that the verse warns them of God's established practice toward those who deny the messengers, while consoling the Prophet. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the outcome refers to the destruction of 'Ad, Thamud and others, and that the strength mentioned refers to bodily vigour and wealth. Al-Razi stresses that human strength cannot prevail against God's will and offers two readings of the phrase that God cannot be frustrated: either as an illustration that the earlier peoples could not overcome Him, or as a rebuttal to those who imagine that cunning can save them.

Disagreements mainly concern the meaning of travel. Al-Shawkani and al-Baydawi take it as the trade journeys to Syria, Yemen and Iraq, during which the traces of destroyed peoples could be seen. Ibn 'Uthaymin distinguishes travel of the heart, through reflection on history, from travel on foot to the ruins, and advises that the latter should be undertaken with weeping. Ibn 'Ashur highlights the phrasing 'while they were', which evokes the strength of those earlier peoples. Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan mention grammatical and recitation debates without drawing consequences for the general meaning.

Finally, commentators agree that the closing remarks on God's forbearance in delaying punishment until an appointed term belong to the same logic of justice and respite.

This verse says that if God were to punish people immediately for the sins they commit, He would leave no living creature on the earth. Instead, He gives them respite until an appointed term, and when that term arrives, He fully knows His servants and will judge them accordingly. The commentators agree on this general meaning and that the pronoun 'its back' refers to the earth, though some note it is understood from context.

They differ on the word 'dabba', the creature that crawls or walks. Al-Tabari, Ibn Mas'ud (as reported by al-Mawardi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi) and Qatada take it to mean every animal, and Qatada adds that this happened in Noah's time, except those in the ark. Al-Kalbi limits it to humans and jinn, since they are the responsible beings, while Ibn Jurayj, al-Akhfash and al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl restrict it to humans alone. Al-Qurtubi finds the first view more apparent, since it is transmitted from a senior companion.

As for the appointed term, most commentators, including Ibn Kathir, al-Razi, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy, identify it as the Day of Resurrection, whereas Muqatil links it to what is recorded in the Preserved Tablet. Al-Mawardi notes that 'when their term comes' may mean the descent of punishment or the resurrection. Al-Razi adds that the verse consoles the believers.

Al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi say God knows who deserves punishment and who deserves honour, while Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi stress that He will repay each person according to their deeds, good or bad. Ibn 'Abbas states that the verse covers both the obedient and the disobedient. Finally, Yahya ibn Sallam and Abu Hamza al-Thumali read the verse as saying that God may withhold rain, bringing destruction upon everything.
